newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria sets reforms agenda ahead of conference.
newsitem.headline: Algeria sets reforms agenda ahead of conference.

text.p: Algerian President Liamine Zeroual has underlined his drive to build a multiparty democracy but exclude Moslem fundamentalists from the country's political future in a blueprint sent to political leaders.

The blueprint, called Platform for National Understanding, and published on Saturday by the Algerian newspaper al Khabar, reasserts Zeroual's determination to hold general elections in the first half of 1997 preceded by a referendum to amend the constitution.
Behind the planned reforms, lie nearly five years of violence blamed on Moslem fundamentalists in which at least 50,000 people have been killed.
Zeroual's blueprint aims to cut the ground from beneath any political party supporting violence and bring into line those who have shown any sympathy for the fundamentalists.

"Violence is a negation of democracy and thus in the future winning and holding power will only be achieved in the framework of respect for the law and through elections in freedom, democracy and transparency according to the people's freedom, willingness and sovereignty," the blueprint states.

The platform, which sets out the lines of a multiparty system, is expected to be adopted by more than 20 political parties including moderate Islamists in a national conference in Algiers on September 14 and 15.
It states that Islam, the Arabic language and Berber culture belong to all Algerians and should be shielded from political use by those seeking to gain or hold power.
"Islam, our religion, must be spared any behaviour or manoeuvre which may cause strife and must be protected from any political use," the blueprint says.
It insists that the state has to promote and care about Islamic values based on "tolerance, equity, brotherhood, freedom, justice and progress", in bid to cut the ground from under Islamists.
The Algerian authorities blame radical Islamists for hijacking the faith of the country's 28 million Moslem as a weapon to seek power.
The North African country erupted into violence in early 1992 when authorities scrapped a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.

Radical Moslem fundamentalists were excluded from Zeroual's talks to prepare the national conference. One of the main secular opposition parties, the Socialist Forces Front (FFS), walked out of the last talks between presidential officials and political leaders, during which recommendations for the national conference were drawn up.
The FFS leaders accused Zeroual of trying to forge an "anti- Islamist front" rather than seek a solution to end the violence.
The platform calls on politicians to commit themselves to rejecting violence.

The platform also envisages local elections being held in the second part of next year in another move to exclude fundamentalists whose outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) took power in more than half the nation's townhalls in 1990.
